stimuli.text: The function $$g$$ is differentiable. Selected values of $$g$$ are shown.
Let $$R$$ be the region enclosed by the graphs of $$f(x) = 2\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$$ and $$g(x) = x^2 - 1$$.

A particle moves in the xy-plane so that for $$0 \leq t \leq 3$$, $$\frac{dx}{dt} = 2\sin\left(\frac{t^2}{5}\right) + 0.5$$ and $$\frac{dy}{dt} = \cos(t)\,e^{t/4}$$. At $$t = 0$$ the particle is at $$(0, 3)$$.
People enter an amusement park at a rate modeled by a differentiable function $$P$$, where $$P(t)$$ is measured in people per minute and $$t$$ is measured in minutes. Selected values are shown.
Consider the curve given by $$x^2 + xy + y^2 = 3$$.
Consider the differential equation $$\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x(y - 1)$$. Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the particular solution with $$f(1) = 2$$.
A function $$f$$ has derivatives of all orders. Selected values are $$f(2) = 1$$, $$f'(2) = 2$$, $$f''(2) = 1$$ and $$f'''(2) = -5$$. For all $$x$$, $$|f^{(4)}(x)| \leq 30$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_{1}^{4} \left(3x^{2} - 6x - 2\right)dx$$?

options.why: This subtracts values of the integrand instead of an antiderivative.
Correct. An antiderivative is $$F(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 2x$$; $$F(4) - F(1) = 12$$.
This is F(b) only; subtract F(a) as well.
This adds F(a) instead of subtracting it.

questions.explanation: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $$\int_{1}^{4} f(x)\,dx = F(4) - F(1)$$ with $$F(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 2x$$. That is $$8 - (-4) = 12$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = 2x^{3} - 18x^{2} + 48x$$. At what value of $$x$$ does $$f$$ have a relative maximum?

options.why: $$f(0) = 0$$, but $$f'(0)$$ is not zero, so this is not a critical point.
Correct. $$f'(x) = 6(x - 2)(x - 4)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$x = 2$$.
At this critical point $$f'$$ changes from negative to positive, which gives a relative minimum.
This is where f″ = 0 (the inflection point), not a critical point.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = 6x^2 - 36x + 48 = 6(x - 2)(x - 4)$$. Testing signs: $$f'$$ is positive left of $$2$$, negative between $$2$$ and $$4$$, positive right of $$4$$. So there is a relative maximum at $$2$$ and a relative minimum at $$4$$.

questions.stem: A population $$P$$ grows according to $$\frac{dP}{dt} = kP$$, and it doubles every 3 years. If $$P(0) = 200$$, what is $$P(6)$$?

options.why: This treats each year as a doubling period.
This adds the original amount once per period (linear growth); exponential growth multiplies by 2 each period.
Correct. $$6$$ years is 2 doubling periods, so the population is multiplied by $$2^{2}$$.
This counts only one doubling period.

questions.explanation: The solution is $$P(t) = 200 \cdot 2^{t/3}$$. So $$P(6) = 200 \cdot 2^{2} = 800$$.

options.why: This multiplies the derivatives of the two factors and then drops the exponential.
This differentiates only the exponential factor.

questions.stem: At what value of $$x$$ does the graph of $$f(x) = -x^{3} + 3x^{2} + 3x$$ have a point of inflection?

options.why: Correct. $$f''(x) = -6x + 6$$ is zero and changes sign at $$x = 1$$.
Inflection points are where f″ changes sign, not where f″ has its constant term.
Sign error when solving f″(x) = 0.
This is −b/(2a), the vertex formula for a parabola, applied to the cubic's coefficients. Set f″(x) = 0 instead.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = -3x^{2} + 6x + 3$$ and $$f''(x) = -6x + 6$$. $$f''$$ is linear, so it changes sign at its zero, $$x = 1$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{2x^2}\right)$$?

options.why: This leaves out the derivative of the inside function.
Correct. This is the chain rule: the derivative of the outer function, evaluated at the inside, times the derivative of the inside.
This differentiates the inside but then substitutes it incorrectly into the outer derivative.
This makes a sign or coefficient error in the outer derivative.

questions.explanation: Treat $$e^{2x^2}$$ as a composite and apply the chain rule: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{2x^2}\right) = 4xe^{2x^2}$$.

options.why: Correct. $$\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \frac{15}{-2}$$.

options.why: Correct. When f″(c) = 0 the Second Derivative Test is inconclusive: $$x^3$$, $$x^4$$ and $$-x^4$$ all have f′(0) = f″(0) = 0.
$$-x^4$$ has a maximum, but $$x^4$$ has a minimum with the same conditions.
$$x^4$$ has a minimum, but $$-x^4$$ has a maximum with the same conditions.

questions.stem: Which of the following gives the area of the region enclosed by the polar curve $$r = 5 + 2\sin\theta$$?

options.why: The radius must be squared.
Correct. Polar area is half the integral of $$r^2$$ over one full trace.
Since $$r > 0$$ for every angle, the curve is traced once over $$[0, 2\pi]$$, not $$[0, \pi]$$.
This leaves out the factor $$\frac{1}{2}$$.

questions.explanation: $$A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta r^2\,d\theta$$. Because $$5 > 2$$, $$r > 0$$ for all $$\theta$$ and the curve closes after $$2\pi$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{1} x\left(x^2 + 2\right)^{3}dx$$?

options.why: After substituting, the limits must change to u-values (from c to 1 + c), not stay 0 to 1.
Correct. With $$u = x^2 + 2$$, $$du = 2x\,dx$$, the integral is $$\frac{1}{2}\int_{2}^{3} u^{3}\,du$$.
This evaluates only at the upper limit.
This forgets the factor $$\frac{1}{2}$$ from $$du = 2x\,dx$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x + 36} - 6}{x}$$?

options.why: This forgets that the conjugate denominator is $$\sqrt{x + 36} + 6$$, which approaches $$12$$, not $$6$$.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, an indeterminate form.
Correct. Rationalizing gives $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 36} + 6}$$, which approaches $$\frac{1}{12}$$.
The expression is undefined at 0, but rationalizing shows the outputs approach a single number.

questions.explanation: Multiply by $$\frac{\sqrt{x + 36} + 6}{\sqrt{x + 36} + 6}$$. The numerator becomes $$x$$, which cancels, leaving $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 36} + 6} \to \frac{1}{12}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_{3}^{\infty} \frac{1}{x^{5}}\,dx$$?

options.why: A p-integral to infinity converges when $$p > 1$$; here $$p = 5$$.
This uses the lower limit 1 instead of $$3$$.
Correct. $$\lim_{b \to \infty}\left[\frac{x^{-4}}{-4}\right]_{3}^{b} = \frac{1}{4\cdot 3^{4}}$$.
This raises the power instead of lowering it.

questions.explanation: Write it as a limit: $$\lim_{b \to \infty}\int_{3}^{b} x^{-5}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty}\left(\frac{1}{4\cdot 3^{4}} - \frac{1}{4b^{4}}\right)$$.

options.why: Correct. Integration by parts, then evaluate at both limits.

questions.stem: What is the interval of convergence of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(x - 3)^n}{n\cdot 5^n}$$?

options.why: The radius is 5, from the factor $$5^n$$.
The endpoints are reversed: the right endpoint gives the divergent harmonic series.
Correct. Ratio test gives $$|x - 3| < 5$$; the left endpoint gives an alternating harmonic series (converges), the right endpoint the harmonic series (diverges).
The left endpoint gives $$\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$, which converges.

questions.explanation: Ratio: $$\left|\frac{(x - 3)^{n+1}}{(n + 1)5^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{n\,5^n}{(x - 3)^n}\right| \to \frac{|x - 3|}{5}$$, so $$|x - 3| < 5$$. At $$x = 8$$: $$\sum \frac{1}{n}$$ diverges. At $$x = -2$$: $$\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$ converges.

options.why: The numerator is not the derivative of the denominator, so this is not a logarithm.

options.why: This counts the backward part twice.
This is the displacement; it subtracts the distance traveled backward.

This is the velocity at the final time.

questions.stem: A function $$f$$ has $$f(-2) = 5$$, $$f'(-2) = -6$$, $$f''(-2) = -7$$ and $$f'''(-2) = 10$$. What is the coefficient of $$(x + 2)^3$$ in the Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = -2$$?

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{6x} - 1}{3x}$$?

options.why: This differentiates the numerator and denominator but then inverts the ratio, or applies the rule incorrectly.

questions.explanation: Direct substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$. Differentiate the numerator and denominator separately (L'Hospital's Rule): $$\frac{6e^{6x}}{3}$$, which gives $$2$$.

questions.stem: Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the solution to $$\frac{dy}{dx} = x^2 - y$$ passing through the point $$(1, 2)$$. What is $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ at that point?

questions.stem:
Which of the following series converge?

I. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n}{n + 1}$$

II. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt{n}}$$

III. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2 + 4}$$

options.why: Check each series with an appropriate test: I diverges, II converges, III converges.
Check each series with an appropriate test: I diverges, II converges, III converges.

Correct. I: diverges (terms approach 1, not 0 (nth term test)). II: converges (alternating series test, but p = 1/2 for the absolute values). III: converges (smaller than the convergent p-series with p = 2).
Check each series with an appropriate test: I diverges, II converges, III converges.

questions.explanation: Series I diverges: terms approach 1, not 0 (nth term test). Series II converges: alternating series test, but p = 1/2 for the absolute values. Series III converges: smaller than the convergent p-series with p = 2.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx - 11 & x < 2 \\ x^{2} - 5 & x \geq 2 \end{cases}$$ where $$k$$ is a constant. For what value of $$k$$ is $$f$$ continuous at $$x = 2$$?

questions.stem: For the curve $$x = t^2$$, $$y = t^{3} + 6t$$, what is $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ at $$t = -1$$?

options.why: This is $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$, the first derivative.

questions.stem: A 10-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall. The bottom of the ladder slides away from the wall at a constant rate of 2 feet per second. How fast is the top of the ladder moving, in feet per second, when the bottom is 6 feet from the wall?

options.why: The two ends do not move at the same speed; their rates depend on the position.

Correct. $$x^2 + y^2 = 100$$ gives $$x\frac{dx}{dt} + y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$$. With $$x = 6$$, $$y = 8$$, $$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{6(2)}{8}$$.

questions.explanation: Let $$x$$ be the distance from the wall and $$y$$ the height. $$2x x' + 2y y' = 0$$, so $$y' = -\frac{x x'}{y} = -\frac{6 \cdot 2}{8} = -\frac{3}{2}$$ feet per second (the top is moving down).

parts.prompt: Must there be a time $$c$$, for $$3 < c < 9$$, such that $$P'(c) = 0$$? Justify your answer.
